questions.q: What does a cost adjustment change on an asset?
options: The asset's recorded cost after it has already been added
questions.explain: A cost adjustment increases or decreases an asset's recorded cost after its original addition, which changes its depreciable basis going forward.

questions.q: A $120,000 asset's cost is increased by $15,000 to $135,000. With a $20,000 salvage value and 10-year life, what is the new annual straight-line depreciation?
questions.explain: ($135,000 - $20,000) / 10 = $11,500, the corrected annual depreciation after the cost increase.

questions.q: What effect does a cost decrease have on an asset's depreciation history?
options: It has no effect on past depreciation
It can only be applied in a tax book
It may mean the asset was over-depreciated relative to the corrected, lower cost
questions.explain: A cost decrease shrinks the depreciable basis, which can mean too much depreciation was already taken relative to the corrected cost, triggering a reverse catch-up.

questions.q: Why might a mass addition line merged into an existing asset (Lesson 14) be considered a form of cost adjustment?
options: Because merging always decreases an asset's cost
Because merged lines are never posted
Because merging changes an asset's location, not its cost
Because merging adds the line's amount as additional cost on the existing asset rather than creating a new asset
questions.explain: A merged mass addition line increases an existing asset's cost rather than creating a separate asset, which is the same type of change a cost adjustment makes.

questions.q: Why do many implementations place a time window or approval threshold around cost adjustments?
options: Because cost adjustments are illegal after the fiscal year ends
Because cost adjustments can only be made to tax books
Because Oracle Fusion Assets limits each asset to one adjustment ever
Because a late adjustment, made after most of an asset's life has depreciated, produces a larger and more disruptive catch-up calculation
questions.explain: Catching cost issues early keeps the resulting catch-up calculation small; a late adjustment produces a much larger, more disruptive correction.
